Well Chris, you've given me the opportunity so I'm going to take it.  Check out my paper here:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.1618/full

Seriously though, I used GVS in the occupancy models in that paper and it worked well.  But the models were simple, covariates were only continuous, and there were no interactions.

In other applications that I've used with categorical covariates and interactions, you need to use an effects parameterization with "sum to zero contrasts" so that estimation of the intercept is the same under all model structures.  If you don't take this approach the parameters might mix poorly as the sampler gets stuck in a bad parameter space and the intercept becomes multi-modal.  For example:

f(y) = b0 + b1*x*g

Here, f(y) is described by a linear model with intercept b0, regression coefficient b1, covariate x, and coefficient indicator g.  If x is continuous and standardized, then b0 does not change whether or not b1 is included (g=0 or g=1), as it represents the grand mean of y.  On the other hand, if x is a binary category, then b0 is the mean for when x=0.  But if b1 is excluded (g=0), b0 is now the grand mean.  So if your model suggests that b1 should included some proportion of the time, then the posterior for b0 will be a mix of the grand mean and the x=0 mean.  "Sum to zero" contrasts would turn x into -1 and 1, instead of 0 and 1.  This allows the intercept to be the same regardless of b1's inclusion.

Interactions are an entirely different problem and tricky, especially if you have a 3-way interaction.  The paper below generally takes an ANOVA-like approach where factors are either included or not, but differences within factors are not considered:
Ntzoufras, I. 2002. Gibbs variable selection using BUGS. Journal of Statistical Software 7:1-19.

I'd be interested in hearing more thoughts on this though.

Hi Chris,

If I understand well, you are using the model selection procedure called (in different ways depending on the source) 'product space' method, or 'Carlin and Chib' method, or 'trans-dimensional' method or 'product space search' method. In many situations, this method seems to be very sensitive to the values of the priors and often the algorithm gets stuck, only picks one model (usually the most supported by the data) and does not explore model space adequately (i.e. you end up with too few transitions between states of different dimension = models, and thus you need a lot of iterations). Chapter 10 of Kruschke (2011) book and Tenan et al (2014, Ecol Modell) give different suggestions on what to do.

I personally prefer the Gibbs Variable selection (GVS) approach (or the similar SSVS method by George and McCulloch) and I made use of it with different models (occupancy models included) to select potential predictors simultaniously on the state and observation model, without any apparent problem. Usually the GVS approach (with the specification of pseudo-priors) achieves better mixing for the indicator variables than the Kuo & Mallick approach (without pseudo-priors). My experience on that is very limited though.

Good luck!
Simone

Chris, I completely agree that that model space prior seems more straightforward and intuitive.  And I will admit that the problem Simone describes with the sampler getting stuck is not completely solved by GVS, at least in my experience.  I've had indicators get stuck at 1 within a certain chain, resulting in a posterior probability of 1 for only that chain, despite probabilities <1 for other chains.  My pragmatic solution was to keep running additional model fits and essentially make inferences off 10s of chains.

I'm attaching some notes and code for a recent application to multi-state mark-recovery (just the indicator priors).  I had 3 factors, with up to a 3-way interaction for both survival probability and mortality cause.  I treated each model component separate, which I think you should do for detection and occupancy.  In restricting the main effects to be present with any interactions, there ended up being 19 models so a 1/19=0.053 prior for each.  Working backward, that meant the 3-way interaction model (#19) had a prior of 0.053 and then it goes on from there, using conditional specifications.  I'm not entirely certain this is correct or even the most efficient but if you run this code without any likelihood connection to the g indicators, the posterior probabilities for each model structure will be 0.053.  And my results seemed more than reasonable.

Here are the notes for mapping the model structures:

# model matrix
# 1    2     3    4    5         6         7        8
# int  site  sex  age  site:sex  site:age  sex:age  site:sex:age
# 0    A     B    C    AB        AC        BC       ABC

#term   g
#0      1
#A      2
#B      3
#C      4
#AB     5
#BC     6
#AC     7
#ABC    8

#m  terms       terms#
#1  0           1
#2  A           12
#3  B           13
#4  A+B         123
#5  C           14
#6  A+C         124
#7  B+C         134
#8  A+B+C       1234
#9  AB          1235
#10 AC          1246
#11 BC          1347
#12 AB+C        12345
#13 AC+B        12346
#14 AB+AC       123456
#15 BC+A        12347
#16 AB+BC       123457
#17 BC+AC       123467
#18 AB+BC+AC    1234567
#19 ABC         12345678

And here are the priors used in the code.  You have to map indicators to regression coefficients in situations where factors have >2 levels.  That is described in the Ntzoufras (2002) paper.  For instance, my factors A and C had 3 levels each (2 for B), resulting in 18 regression coefficients:

# GVS indicators
for(p in 1:2){
  g[p,8]~dbern(0.053) #set to ~dbern(1) to get pseudopriors from global fit
  # Pr(g7|g8)
  p.g7[p] <- (1-g[p,8])*0.2777 + g[p,8]
  g[p,7]~dbern(p.g7[p])
  # Pr(g6|g7,g8)
  p.g6[p] <- (0.231^(1-g[p,7]))*(0.4^g[p,7])*(1-g[p,8]) + g[p,8]
  g[p,6]~dbern(p.g6[p])
  g6g7[p] <- g[p,6]+g[p,7]
  # Pr(g5|g6,g7,g8)
  p.g5[p] <- (0.2^equals(g6g7[p],0))*(0.333^equals(g6g7[p],1))*(0.5^equals(g6g7[p],2))*(1-g[p,8]) + g[p,8]
  g[p,5]~dbern(p.g5[p])
  g5g7[p] <- g[p,5]+g[p,7]
  g5g6[p] <- g[p,5]+g[p,6]
  # Pr(g4|g6,g7)
  p.g4[p] <- equals(g6g7[p],0)*0.5 + (1-equals(g6g7[p],0))
  # Pr(g3|g5,g7)
  p.g3[p] <- equals(g5g7[p],0)*0.5 + (1-equals(g5g7[p],0))
  # Pr(g2|g5,g6)
  p.g2[p] <- equals(g5g6[p],0)*0.5 + (1-equals(g5g6[p],0))
  g[p,4]~dbern(p.g4[p])
  g[p,3]~dbern(p.g3[p])
  g[p,2]~dbern(p.g2[p])
  g[p,1]~dbern(1)
}

for(j in 1:18){
  for(p in 1:2){
    gtemp[p,j] <- g[p,pos[j]]
}}

And I will admit that the problem Simone describes with the sampler getting stuck is not completely solved by GVS, at least in my experience.  I've had indicators get stuck at 1 within a certain chain, resulting in a posterior probability of 1 for only that chain, despite probabilities <1 for other chains.  My pragmatic solution was to keep running additional model fits and essentially make inferences off 10s of chains.

I'm attaching some notes and code for a recent application to multi-state mark-recovery (just the indicator priors).  I had 3 factors, with up to a 3-way interaction for both survival probability and mortality cause.  I treated each model component separate, which I think you should do for detection and occupancy.  In restricting the main effects to be present with any interactions, there ended up being 19 models so a 1/19=0.053 prior for each.  Working backward, that meant the 3-way interaction model (#19) had a prior of 0.053 and then it goes on from there, using conditional specifications.  I'm not entirely certain this is correct or even the most efficient but if you run this code without any likelihood connection to the g indicators, the posterior probabilities for each model structure will be 0.053.  And my results seemed more than reasonable.

Here are the notes for mapping the model structures:

# model matrix
# 1    2     3    4    5         6         7        8
# int  site  sex  age  site:sex  site:age  sex:age  site:sex:age
# 0    A     B    C    AB        AC        BC       ABC

#term   g
#0      1
#A      2
#B      3
#C      4
#AB     5
#BC     6
#AC     7
#ABC    8

#m  terms       terms#
#1  0           1
#2  A           12
#3  B           13
#4  A+B         123
#5  C           14
#6  A+C         124
#7  B+C         134
#8  A+B+C       1234
#9  AB          1235
#10 AC          1246
#11 BC          1347
#12 AB+C        12345
#13 AC+B        12346
#14 AB+AC       123456
#15 BC+A        12347
#16 AB+BC       123457
#17 BC+AC       123467
#18 AB+BC+AC    1234567
#19 ABC         12345678

And here are the priors used in the code.  You have to map indicators to regression coefficients in situations where factors have >2 levels.  That is described in the Ntzoufras (2002) paper.  For instance, my factors A and C had 3 levels each (2 for B), resulting in 18 regression coefficients:

# GVS indicators
for(p in 1:2){
  g[p,8]~dbern(0.053) #set to ~dbern(1) to get pseudopriors from global fit
  # Pr(g7|g8)
  p.g7[p] <- (1-g[p,8])*0.2777 + g[p,8]
  g[p,7]~dbern(p.g7[p])
  # Pr(g6|g7,g8)
  p.g6[p] <- (0.231^(1-g[p,7]))*(0.4^g[p,7])*(1-g[p,8]) + g[p,8]
  g[p,6]~dbern(p.g6[p])
  g6g7[p] <- g[p,6]+g[p,7]
  # Pr(g5|g6,g7,g8)
  p.g5[p] <- (0.2^equals(g6g7[p],0))*(0.333^equals(g6g7[p],1))*(0.5^equals(g6g7[p],2))*(1-g[p,8]) + g[p,8]
  g[p,5]~dbern(p.g5[p])
  g5g7[p] <- g[p,5]+g[p,7]
  g5g6[p] <- g[p,5]+g[p,6]
  # Pr(g4|g6,g7)
  p.g4[p] <- equals(g6g7[p],0)*0.5 + (1-equals(g6g7[p],0))
  # Pr(g3|g5,g7)
  p.g3[p] <- equals(g5g7[p],0)*0.5 + (1-equals(g5g7[p],0))
  # Pr(g2|g5,g6)
  p.g2[p] <- equals(g5g6[p],0)*0.5 + (1-equals(g5g6[p],0))
  g[p,4]~dbern(p.g4[p])
  g[p,3]~dbern(p.g3[p])
  g[p,2]~dbern(p.g2[p])
  g[p,1]~dbern(1)
}

for(j in 1:18){
  for(p in 1:2){
    gtemp[p,j] <- g[p,pos[j]]
}}

Hi Simone, my code was missing other parts of the model that obviate the need for g[p,1].  I used a design matrix, x, and vector multiplication in JAGS to create the linear predictor:

X.beta <- x %*% (beta[p,]*gtemp[p,])

This way, the bookkeeping for psuedopriors is simplified when you fit the global model before the GVS model, as beta is a single object.  But yes, you could simply separate the intercept entirely from the model selection process since it does not change.

messages.subject_clean: AW: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

thanks very much to several people who have taken the time to reply to my question about the reasons for the undesirable end-of-series behavior in an analysis of citizen-science data with a dynamic occupancy model and sorry for taking so long in summarizing.

Three people suggested that this may be due to reduced information available about parameters at the start or the end of a Markovian model than in the middle of a series and to shrinkage towards the mean of the random year effects for colonization and persistence. One person suggested there may be cycles in the values of the two dynamics parameters (but did say clearly that this was an observation unrelated to uor problem. Two persons suggested that there may be end of series problems with parameter identifiability similar to what occurs in the CJS and related multi-state models.

>From this and from additional simulations that my colleague Nicolas Strebel ran we now think that the first answer is actually the correct one. Indeed, we model the annual parameters for persistence and colonization (on the logit scale) as draws from a normal distribution with a constant mean and constant variance, that is, as random effects. So if there is some trend in either persistence or colonization over time, then the shrinkage towards the mean hyperparameter will tend to obscure this trend at the end. When more years are added to the series, we get more information about the parameters for those same years and the effect of the random-effects prior mean declines.

I have to admit that I am not so sure about the other explanation offered, about lack of identifiability of the end of series parameters. We have a robust design here, which gives us considerably more information than in the usual CJS/multistate case with a single observation per primary period only.

In any case, thanks to you all for helping us out here. If we meet ever/the next time, the first bottle of beer/glass of wine is on me.

Best regards  ---- Marc

Here is a summary of the replies we got:

>From  Joe Hightower: .... "I often see this pattern in multistate fisheries models for estimating fishing and natural mortality rates from telemetry data.  True states for a simple case are alive, natural death and fishing death.  Observed states for that model are alive, natural death, and not detected. Fishing mortality typically trends up at the end of a study because the model cannot decide whether fish that are not detected for a period or two have been harvested or simply missed.  Adding another occasion (ours are typically months) almost always pulls those fishing mortality rates down because some of the missing fish get detected.  The details would vary depending on temporal patterns in fishing mortality and detection probability, and how detection probabilities were estimated (independently or drawn from a shared distribution).  I don't think my example is a true bias but simply the influence of the priors (U(01) for detection probabilities, mortality rates are uninformative in log-scale), especially since sample sizes tend to be low at the end of a study.  We typically deal with this issue by doing additional searches at the end or extending the monitoring period beyond the true period of interest for the study."

>From Nathanael Lichti: " Rob Swihart passed this along to his lab group.  My first instinct is that this looks like the difference between (in time series jargon) a filtered estimate and a smoothed estimate.  For the terminal value in the series, you’re modeling

A = L(z_t | z_[1, …, t -1], phi_t, gamma_t) = Bern(z_t | z_[t – 1] * phi_t + (1 – z_[t – 1]) * gamma_t)

But values within the series are constrained from above (i.e., the future) as well as below. For t = T -1,

L(z_t | z_[1, …, t -1], z_[t+1]) = A * P(z_[t + 1] | z_[1, …, t], phi_[t+1], gamma_[t+1])

Since these are hierarchical estimates, I would bet that what looks like lower values is actually reversion to the mean as a result of having less constraint on the terminal value."

>From John Clare: " First thought (total shot in the dark): are you imposing a random effect structure on gamma?  Could the discrepancies at the end of the time series relate to hyper-parameter values and indirectly, the mean and variance up until the last observation?  To my eye, it looks like the end of the time-series represent departures from the longer term mean and variance, and that perhaps the addition of more years within certain models is shifting hyper-parameter values.  "

>From Eduardo Carrillo-Rubio: " Looking at your time series, I noticed a cyclical pattern every 5 years or so in gamma (slightly noticeable in phi and also in psi, although less obvious due to a slight positive trend) that seems consistent with the last years of your time series as well. I'm sure you guys thought about it before, but would it be possible that your estimates are correctly showing a natural fluctuation in the data?

I find that the last years in your time series estimates (especially gamma) are not entirely unreasonable if you think there could be a natural fluctuation, although I do see why these could be puzzling. Is there any evidence of a relationship between gamma at t+1 and t? e.g., would gamma increase in year t+1 given that it was also high in year t? "

>From Christian Roy: " It's difficult to judge without the full model. But this problem seems similar to the non-identifiability problems that plague some banding data analysis. Under some models the parameters reported for the last years are always wrong...

I would dig in that direction since the description of your model seems to imply that you have some parameters that are dependent on their previous state (i.e, the value of t is dependent on t-1). "

>From Guillaume Souchay: " Like Christian, your issue looks very similar to identifiability issue usually met in capture-recapture analysis, especially with models dealing with temporary emigration. One big issue is when temporary emigration is completely random, then identifiability issue arises. If temporary emigration is really markovian (depending on former state), then the estimates were unbiased. In any case, survival was unbiased. You can ask to your quasi-desk-neighbour, Michi, who wrote a paper about identification issues in such model (Schaub et al 2004 Ecology, 85, 2107-2113, see also Kendall & Nichols 2002 Ecology, 83, 3276-3284 with a robust design sampling).

Similarly, in your case, persistence seems to be unbiased as survival in temporary emigration models but transitions (colonization and extinction) could be biased using unconditional dynamic occupancy model (random process)."

An: hmec...@googlegroups.com
Cc: Sattler Thomas; Strebel Nicolas
Betreff: vexing problem with dynamic occupancy model

Dear all,

in an application of dynamic occupancy models (MacKenzie et al., Ecology, 2003) to a typical citizen-science data set, my colleagues Nicolas Strebel, Thomas Sattler and I have encountered a vexing problem with something that we consider to be bias in the estimates for the final years of a series. The problem is that the estimate of psi (occupancy) for a given year t, when it is the final year in the series, is typically lower than the estimate for that same year when we add one year of data, i.e., when the series extends to t + 1 : in this case, the estimate for year t typically becomes higher. And it becomes higher still when we add a second year of data, i.e., when the series extends until year t+2.

You can see this well in the attached figures for the analysis of one species (wood lark), please focus on the first of the two plots on each page. BLUE shows the estimates (with 95% CRIs) based on the time series from 1990-2011, RED is that for the analysis of the time series until 2012 and black is that for the analysis of the time series until 2013. In the triple of estimates for the years 2009, 2010 and 2011 you can see that the estimates for those years move UP when an additional year of data is added to the series (and the analysis). This is a Bayesian analysis with JAGS, with U(0,1) priors on the probabilities.

When looking at the estimates for persistence (phi) and colonization (gamma), we find the same pattern in colonization, but not in persistence.

Using many different ways of subsetting the full data set as well as simulation we have tried to find out the reason for it, but we are still not sure about it. Perhaps somebody of you sees why this is or has a hunch ? Let’s say that the first person who finds out why this is gets  ... a bottle of beer ? A glass of wine ? Or perhaps even a copy of our upcoming book on hierarchical modeling ? We have to think. But we are desperate ;)

Thanks a lot and and kind regards  ---- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to run an integrated population model combining CMR and point-count data.
I have set up a multi-state model for the CMR data to get survival estimates (by site, age and origin of birds - here <https://groups.google.com/d/topic/hmecology/kNtUL7sTJx0/discussion> is a discussion about the CMR model I'm using) and I have a N-mixture model to estimate total abundance on each site (quite basic with detection as a linear relationship with several covariates and a random effect).
The matrix population model I use is a 2-age classes for wild individuals and also releases individuals, following the study of Sarrazin & Legendre 2000 (Conserv. Biol. 14).
A particularity of our model is that point-counts occur in March and releases in September. Thus, I built "seasonal" matrix population model with 2 intervals: Spring(y) to Autumn(y) and Autumn(y) to Spring(y+1).
For each site, I can estimate total abundance (NTot) as the sum of abundance at each spatial replicate (N.rep) from the N-mixture model. The total abundance is also the sum of the 3 classes (juv and ad wild individuals + releases). To deal with that, and because I could not define twice total abundance, the trick was to use a multinomial distribution for the abundance of each replicate:
N.rep[i,a,s] ~ dmulti(pi[i,s],NTot[a,s])
NTot[a,s] <- N[1,a,s]+N[2,a,s]+N[3,a,s] #N1, N2 and N3 are number of wild subadults, wild adults and releases subadults respectively
I figured out how to write the model and it's ok for JAGS. The model can be compiled, so, it's a first good point.
The tricky part now is to find good initial values. When running the N-mixture model alone, I used the maximum number of observed individuals as initial values and it works.
However, now, with the new constraints on N.rep (that must also satisfy to constraint associated with the population model), I'm quite stuck to find proper initial values for N.rep...
I have tried several initials values, from the max of observed ind to the real abundance at each replicate, but none is working.

If you have any idea or general tips on how to provide "good" initials values ...

Thanks for the help !

Guillaume

Guillaume,

I ran my IPM through WinBUGS. When it crashed, I chose Model -> Save State. Then I copy and pasted the values used in the sampler, and specified those as inits, and ran the model again. For my issue, the sampler would run a bit, but then crash, but usually one or two of the three chains were alright, just one of them hung things up. So I looked at the three windows with the final values from each chain and made sure not to use the chain with extreme values for the inits.

Seemed to work for me. Then I could transfer those working inits and run in JAGS or whatever other program that may be desirable. Not sure if JAGS has a similar 'save state' option (would assume it does)?

I can't speak to the whether this is theoretically appropriate, but it seemed to produce reasonable results.

Hope this helps a bit!

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using unmarked R package, N-mixture models in particular (function
pcount). As I see the ?pcount help page, total abundance can be easily
reported:

m1 <- pcount(...)
m1r <- ranef(m1)
cat("Modelled abundance: \n")
sum(bup(m1r))

But is it also possible to report its confidence interval?
I know I can get confidence intervals for abundance at separate sites using confint:

confint(m1r, level=0.95)

but this cannot be easily used for the confidence intervals of the total
abundance, since quantile of sum is not necessarily sum of quantiles :-)
(see http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/134976)

So is there any other solution in unmarked?

Thanks,

	Tomas

Dear Tomas,

you can bootstrap the variance of that derived quantity. For this, you will have to write a function that computes the sum either of the BUPs (from ranef()) or else of the predicted abundances (from predict()) for the set of sites you want to consider. Then, you use parboot() to produce a parametric bootstrap sample of that population total.

Kind regards  --  Marc
